entries.text: Morning, sir. The tea is already on the stove, just as it was last night. I didn’t touch the kettle, but the water is hot and ready if you want it.

The tea is a courtesy, but the stomach is an imperative. I have no food to cook, and Ramesh stands before me needing money I do not have. I must be plain about the deficit before I can ask for a solution.

Ramesh, I will take the tea. But I must speak of the groceries. I have no money for the full list you sent. I have only one hundred and twenty-six rupees in my pocket. Can you arrange a minimal purchase with that amount, or must I find the rest before I go out?

Sir, with just one hundred and twenty-six, I cannot manage a proper list of groceries. It is not that I will not help, but the prices are what they are. You must find the rest if you wish to eat properly.

Ramesh speaks the truth of civil society: the system of needs is indifferent to my dignity. With only ₹126, I cannot purchase the staples required for a proper meal, nor can I cover the deficit without the state's money. I must go to the Directorate of Estates to address the identity query and secure the imprest, for the body requires what the state has allotted.

entries.text: You are right, Ramesh. The market does not wait for the philosopher. I will go to the Directorate of Estates to settle the matter of my identity and the funds. Do not prepare anything further until I return.
Understood, sir. I will keep the house quiet and the stove off until you are back. Do not worry about the tea, it is already made.

Ramesh has secured the domestic front; the stove is off, the tea is ready, and the silence is arranged. I am left alone with Hegde, a man who bears my name and watches me with the quiet suspicion of a man whose identity has been stolen by a ghost. I must address him before I leave, for he is the living proof of the error that binds me to this bungalow and this city.

Shri Hegde, since I am to remain here until the Directorate sorts out this clerical catastrophe, I would prefer we not stand in silent antagonism. You are a Joint Secretary; I am a philosopher of no rank. Let us be civil. Do you have any instructions for my conduct, or am I to govern the house by my own discretion?

Sir, if you are going to sit here for weeks, at least learn to use the doorbell instead of knocking like a delivery boy. Ramesh, put the kettle on, I will need a strong chai to survive this conversation.

Hegde’s presence is becoming a nuisance, a living contradiction to the file’s error. I cannot let him settle into the rhythm of the house; he must be reminded that he is the one who belongs to the city, not me. I will take the chai he requests, but I will use the moment to press the matter of his departure before I leave for the Directorate.

The kettle is already on, Shri Hegde. But do not mistake this for hospitality. Your presence here is an administrative accident, and I intend to correct the record at the Directorate this morning. Perhaps you will find the walk to the city more invigorating than the silence of this bungalow.

You say 'correct the record,' but you haven't even finished your morning chai, sir. Go on, then, walk to the city and let the cold air clear your head; I will be here, filing the paperwork that actually exists.

The bureaucratic machinery is closed, and the market of needs is not yet awake. I am trapped in the interim, the space between the opening of one institution and the other. I will return to the bungalow; the tea is still warm, and I have the hour to sit with the absurdity of my name in a file that does not belong to me. It is a moment of pure waiting, where the mind must turn upon itself.

The Directorate is closed for the holiday, and Hegde’s presence makes the house feel like a waiting room rather than a home. I cannot walk to a place that is shut, and the market is still quiet. I shall sit with Hegde, perhaps in a gruff courtesy, and wait for the city to wake up so I may address this absurdity.
The compound walls along the road are limewashed white with a black band at the foot, and every gate carries its number in black paint and a brass plate gone green at the corners.

It is nearly eleven, and the Directorate remains closed for the holiday, so the identity query must wait. Hegde is still here, a silent witness, and the cold is sharp. I will not waste the morning idling in this waiting room; I shall walk to the Indian Institute of Cinema to observe the city's institutions and perhaps clear my head.
Ramesh, see that the house is kept in order. I am walking to the Institute.
Yes, sir. The place is spotless. I’ll keep the stove ready for your return.

The IIC is open, a rare mercy in this holiday heat. I am at the library, where the quiet is the proper element of thought, though my stomach growls with the impatience of a body that has not been fed in two days. The identity query waits at the Directorate, but here I might find a newspaper or a book to settle the mind before the afternoon walk. I shall sit for a while, if the guard permits, and let the dust settle.
On the board by the entrance, typed notices curl at their corners under coloured pins, and last month's programme still shows through this month's.

The notices curl like dead leaves, a small decay in the system of the library. I have not eaten since yesterday morning, and the heat is beginning to press against the bandhgala. The plan for the Directorate is dead for today; the body, however, still operates by its own necessity. I must eat, or the rest of the day is a mere abstraction.

It is midday, and the plan called for a meal here. I have not eaten in twenty-five hours, and the body, that stubborn medium of spirit, demands its due. I see Sunil and the bookseller; I shall take chai and a samosa to sustain the walk ahead. The wine is beyond my current means, a reminder of the friction between desire and cash.
Sunil, good afternoon. A cup of chai and a samosa, please.
Fifty rupees, same as yesterday. You know the drill by now, sir. Sit, the stove is already hot.

The system of needs is punctual; it does not ask for my identity, only my coin. I am hungry after a long morning of administrative friction, and the body’s demand is the first step of reason. I will eat, and then I shall look for the wine, if the purse permits, for a mind requires both bread and a little poison to think clearly.

shelf.ref: Introduction: the Geographical Basis of History

entries.text: Thank you, Sunil. The rhythm is comforting. I will take this here, if you please.
Aaj thanda hai na? Wrap it up, sir, don't get sick. I'll keep the kettle going if you need another later.

The chill in the air is a small check on the body, and the kindness of the chai-wallah is a minor form of social recognition that costs nothing but attention. I have eaten the samosa, but the hunger for a proper meal remains, and the plan calls for a dhaba lunch if the funds allow, though my pocket holds only the remnant of the morning's chai and snack. I shall settle the account for this small repast and look for a place to sit.
Bahut accha, thank you. The cold is sharp today, indeed.
Sharp, haan? Wind is picking up from the north again. Drink it hot, sir, and don't stand in that draft by the gate.

The wind is a physical force that ignores the boundaries of my philosophical categories, but it is kind to the body. I am still hungry; the samosa was a prelude, not a meal. I have enough for a proper lunch at the dhaba, and perhaps a bottle of wine if the universe is generous, though the dry day makes that a distant hope.

shelf.ref: The Greek World, The Peloponnesian War

entries.text: The wind is certainly sharper than the air in Berlin, even in winter. Sunil, do you know if the dhaba nearby is serving a full lunch? I require more than a samosa to sustain the afternoon.
Berlin? That's far, sir. Yes, Sharma's dhaba is serving the full lunch, dal, rice, roti, all of it. It'll be two hundred and twenty rupees, same as the menu says.

Twenty-six hours without a proper meal is a physical fact that no amount of dialectical reasoning can override. The body demands its due, and the state of hunger is a moment of the negative that must be sublated by the positive act of eating. I have the cash; the transaction is straightforward.
Yes, I shall take the lunch. Please bring it here when it is ready.
Done, sir. I'll send the lad over in ten minutes, don't you worry. Sit tight, the chai is still warm enough to keep the wind out for now.

The dhaba boy is on his way, and the wind is indeed biting, so I shall not stand in the open. I will wait for the food to arrive, as it is the only rational course of action given my physical condition.

The dhaba boy has not returned, and the wind off the canal is sharp enough to make a man reconsider his patience. I have the means to feed myself here and now, and the body does not care for the dignity of waiting. A cup of chai and a samosa will bridge the gap to the dhaba, and I shall not stand in the open any longer.
Sunil, another cup of chai and a samosa, if you please. I am tired of standing in the wind.
Of course, sir. The wind is sharp this afternoon, so a hot cup and a samosa are just what you need. I'll have them ready in a minute.

The wind off the canal is indeed biting, and my stomach, having missed the dhaba, protests with a sharpness that mirrors the air. I shall accept Sunil's hospitality, not out of charity, but because a man cannot think clearly on an empty vessel, and the chai is a small comfort against the Delhi chill.
Thank you, Sunil. The cold is unforgiving today. I shall take the chai and the samosa.
Twenty for the chai, thirty for the samosa, sir. Put your thumb on the cup, it's boiling hot. Don't let that wind get you, you look like a ghost in that bandhgala.

The dhaba has failed me again, and the wind cuts through the thin cotton of my bandhgala. I am left with the samosas, which are at least substantial, and the chai, which Sunil has prepared with a kindness that borders on condescension. I shall eat here, on the spot, rather than wander further into the cold; the steel tumbler is hot to the touch, a small anchor against the biting air.

The dhaba boy has abandoned his post. I shall make do with the samosas, which are at least warm, and your chai, which is a mercy. The wind is indeed unkind, and I am not a ghost, merely a man out of season.
Out of season, ha? The dhaba lad ran off to check the match, left me holding the tongs. Eat while it's hot, sir, the wind won't wait for your philosophy.

The dhaba's absence is a caprice of the particular, but the samosa in my hand is the universal truth of sustenance. I must eat quickly; the wind has no patience for dialectics, and my body, unlike my spirit, demands the immediate. A moment of calm food will steady me for the walk to the gardens.

entries.text: You are right. The wind does not wait, and neither should I.
That's the spirit. Finish up, the match is starting in ten and my ears are going to bleed if I have to listen to the commentary again.

Sunil’s eagerness to escape my presence for the sake of a match is a charming inversion of the master-servant relation; I am the one being dismissed, not the other way around. The samosa is finished, and with ₹26 in my pocket I cannot afford the luxury of lingering or the wine I sought earlier. I shall withdraw with dignity before the commentary begins.
Enjoy the match, Sunil. The commentary will be less painful if you are not forced to listen to it against your will.
Aye, aye, philosopher. You think I don't know who's talking? I've got my own little radio here if I want the agony. You go on and finish your tea before it goes cold.

The afternoon is quiet, and my stomach, despite the samosa, feels a hollow echo of the morning's discipline. I have a debt to Ramesh that weighs on me as much as the identity query does on the Directorate. I will address the matter of his wages directly, for a servant's trust is the foundation of the household's order, and I cannot let it crumble over a few rupees.

Ramesh, before you go, we must speak of the accounts. You are owed four thousand five hundred rupees. I have only twenty-six in my pocket, but I will not let this debt stand unacknowledged while I draw on the state's imprest. I will include your full due in the next voucher I submit to the Directorate. Until then, you have my word, which is as good as the paper I sign.
Sir, do not worry about the money, the Directorate will handle the official payments. Please take care on your walk to the Institute, the evening will be cool.

Ramesh’s assurance that the Directorate will handle the official payments is a convenient fiction, but I accept the gesture of care. The Institute is open, and a change of air is preferable to the hollow echo in my stomach. I shall walk now, before the light fails completely.
Thank you, Ramesh. I shall be careful.
Hmph. Just keep your own feet on the path, sir. The tea will be hot when you get back.

The IIC library is a place of quiet order, a necessary counterweight to the chaos of the identity query. I have little cash, but I have time, and the afternoon light is already thinning on the lawns. I will sit here and let the mind settle before the walk home, perhaps reading to see if the universal can offer any comfort to a man whose particular existence is in bureaucratic limbo.

The hunger is a concrete negation that philosophy cannot dispel with words. I have been here long enough; the library is open, but my body requires the satisfaction of a need that is as rational as any concept. I shall ask the guard where the nearest food can be found, or if there is a canteen, before I continue my wanderings.
Excuse me. I am in need of a meal. Is there a canteen or a place to eat nearby? I have only a small amount of cash.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Sir, I cannot help you with meals here; this is strictly a reading room. Try the canteen in the main block, but honestly, for a small amount, the street food near the Metro station is much better value.

The guard’s suggestion is practical, but the distance to the Metro station is too great for my current state of exhaustion and the meagerness of my purse. I have ₹26, which is insufficient for a proper meal, and I have already eaten snacks. I must return to the bungalow to rest and prepare for Ananya’s lesson in an hour. The hunger will have to wait; the mind requires its own sustenance.
Thank you, but I must return to my residence to prepare for an evening engagement. The library will have to do for now.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Right, I’ll note the time in my log. Just remember to sign out at the desk before you go, sir, or the officer will be on my head.

The day is spent, and the silence in the bungalow is heavy with the weight of the unresolved query. I have walked far enough for the body to complain, and the mind to settle. I will rest here, preparing for the German lesson tomorrow, and let the evening close like a book.

Ramesh stands before me, the stove ready, the house silent. I am too tired to walk further, and the heat of the stove is a small comfort against the cold creeping in with the dark. I will sit for a while, perhaps read a few lines of Protagoras, and let the day settle. The query at the Directorate remains unanswered, but tonight it can wait.
Thank you, Ramesh. The stove is a good idea. I shall take a short rest before the evening lesson.
Rest is good for the head, sir. I will keep the kettle warm, no need to rush.

Thirty-two hours without a proper meal is a condition that defies the dialectic; the body is a stubborn fact that refuses to be sublated by thought. Ramesh offers the comfort of a warm house, but my stomach demands the external world of civil society, specifically the system of needs found in Khan Market. I must go out before the shutters close and the opportunity for sustenance passes.
Ramesh, I will take a short walk to Khan Market. The air is cool, and I require something more substantial than the silence of this room.
Khan Market is a long walk for you, sir. The cold is coming on early this year. I will keep a light snack ready when you return.

The bookseller is still there, his stall a quiet island in the fading light. I have twenty-six rupees in my pocket, a sum that buys a cup of tea or a single newspaper, but not the wine I sought earlier. The body demands fuel; the mind demands order. I will take a samosa and a chai, eating slowly, and perhaps ask the bookseller for a newspaper to read on the walk home, if the price allows.

Good evening. I am in need of a simple meal, as I have not eaten properly in two days. Do you have a samosa and a cup of chai available here? And might I have a newspaper as well, if you have one left?

Good evening, sir. We are a bookshop, not a dhaba, but I suppose I can point you to the place down the lane that serves samosas and chai. As for the newspaper, yes, we have one left, it is forty-five rupees.

The body is a stubborn fact that refuses to be sublated by the spirit of the bookshop. I am thirty-two hours past a proper meal, and the bookseller’s polite deflection to the dhaba is a practical wisdom I must accept. The newspaper is a temptation, but my purse holds only twenty-six rupees; the samosas and chai will cost fifty. I will eat, for the head is empty enough already.
Thank you, sir. The samosas and chai, then. I will return for the paper if my purse permits it.
That’s fine, sir, you take your time. Just watch out for the crows near the dhaba, they are very bold these days.

The bookseller’s warning about the crows is a small, concrete detail, but it reminds me that even in the quiet of the market, nature asserts its own rights. I have twenty-three rupees, which is not enough for a meal, but the air is cool and the light is fading. I will not risk the crows or the dwindling light to eat; I will return home to prepare for the lesson and the dark.

entries.text: Thank you, sir. I shall take your advice. Good evening.
Good evening, sir. The newspaper will be right here when you get back, just don't let those birds get to it first.

The day has drained me, and the cold air in the bungalow makes the fatigue feel heavier, a physical weight that resists the spirit's commands. I have walked enough for one evening; the house, however it is allotted, is where I am for now. I shall sit in the chair by the window and let the silence settle the dust of the market in my mind.

Your letter reached me this morning, a cool drop of Munich rain in the arid heat of my study. It is a strange thing to read the name Niethammer again, two centuries after the ink dried on our last correspondence. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. That you, his descendant, should extend this same recognition to me now, under such bewildering circumstances, is a bond that transcends the mere accident of history. I accept your generosity with the same gratitude I once offered Friedrich, though I must confess that the practical details of my current existence are somewhat more complex than our shared memory suggests.

You ask how I fare in this strange new chapter. I wake each day in a bungalow that belongs, on paper, to a Mr. Hegde, a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. The Directorate of Estates has mistaken my name for his, and while I have written to correct the record, the machinery of the state moves with the slow, deliberate grace of a glacier. My file is currently “gone up for orders,” and I am told to wait fifteen days. In the meantime, I am a ghost in the machine, a particular will suspended between the universal claim of the administration and the immediate necessity of my own body.

The air today is hazy, the index standing at 150, a brown suspension that chokes the sky. I did not go to Lodhi Gardens as I had planned, for the body, even that of a philosopher, cannot breathe in a moral vacuum. I must confess a small defeat today. I went to Lodhi Gardens in the early afternoon, seeking the coolness of the shadows and the observation of the winter light. The domes of the Sayyids and Lodis stand against a sky that is clear and indifferent. I watched the light leave the lawn at six, and it did not linger. In Swabia, an evening lingers at the door like a guest who is reluctant to leave; here, the day is simply dismissed. It is a sharp observation, but it left me with a sense of isolation that I could not quite articulate until I returned home. I walked seven kilometers, and the body is now heavy, a weight that grounds the mind but also slows its movement.

I have been thinking about your distinction between the state as a machine and the ethical life in habit. You are right to wince at my previous 'moral vacuum,' but I find that the bureaucracy here is not merely indifferent; it is actively opaque. I filled out Form 12-B this week, and in that carbon copy, I became Shri G. Hegde. I signed my name as a ghost. The state does not demand my soul; it demands my signature on a fiction. It is a profound indifference, as you say, but it is also a kind of violence against the particular self. Ramesh, my caretaker, does not ask for my identity. He asks for my presence. He leaves with a quiet deference that I accept without ostentation. There is a dignity in that silence that the office lacks. The state demands my identity; Ramesh accepts my existence. The latter is the harder truth to bear, because it offers no title, only a place.

I am well, though the body complains of the cold and the dust. The mind is active, if sometimes frustrated by the resistance of the particular to the universal. I will continue to write.

With warm regards,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel

Dear Mr. Hegel,

Your letter arrived on a grey Tuesday, breaking the monotony of the December light. I read your account of the Directorate with a mixture of amusement and a sharp, familiar recognition. You describe yourself as the subjunctive, a being contingent on the form. My pupils would agree with you. They understand the subjunctive as the mood of the 'what if,' the hypothetical, the wish. It is the tense of potentiality that has not yet hardened into the indicative fact. To be 'if the form is filled' is a terrifying state of suspension, yet it is not empty. It is the space where the will is tested against the indifference of the world.

You mention Mr. Saxena’s demand for an Aadhaar card in the name of Shri G. Hegde. It reminds me of the bureaucratic hurdles we face here, though our machinery is slightly more polite in its opacity. In 1808, Niethammer’s reforms sought to make the state transparent, to align the legal order with the ethical life. I suspect you would find the modern Indian state, with its digital identity and rigid categorization, a fascinating counter-example to his ideals. It is not that the state lacks a soul, but that it has developed a nervous system that is too sensitive to the particular and too blind to the universal. It sees the card, not the man.

I am glad Ramesh provides you with that quiet dignity. Care is a radical act in a world that demands performance. In my classroom, I see teenagers who are terrified of being seen, of being categorized by their grades. Ramesh’s silence offers a respite from that surveillance. It is a form of freedom that does not require a title.

The heat breaking and the cold setting in must be a relief. Please do not overwork yourself in the garden. The mind needs rest as much as it needs clarity. I am preparing a new batch of Latin texts; we are approaching the poetry of the late Republic, where the language begins to crack under the weight of history. I wonder if you will find your own voice changing as you navigate this new existence.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

Dear Mr. Hegel,

Your letter arrived on a crisp Thursday, the air in Munich dry and biting after a week of grey drizzle. I read your account of Lodhi Gardens with a strange pang of recognition. You write that the light leaves the lawn at six and does not linger, whereas in Swabia it stays like a reluctant guest. I know that reluctance well. You frame it as a distinction between mine and the state’s, but I see it as an exercise in finite freedom. To manage a household, to keep the books straight, is to exercise one’s will within the limits of the material world. It is not a lesser form of ethics than the grand declarations of the state; it is the foundation upon which they are built. Ramesh’s quiet efficiency is not merely a respite from the bureaucracy; it is a model of how the universal can be embodied in the particular without becoming abstract. He does not need a title to be free; he is free in the doing.

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter arrived today, a physical object that bridged the silence of my study. I read it by the window as the air cooled to nineteen degrees, a clarity that felt, as you predicted, like a harsh but honest teacher. You speak of the 'ethical weight' of household stewardship, and you are right to correct my tendency to dismiss the particular. I have spent these weeks treating the grocery vouchers and the electricity bills as mere abstractions, obstacles to the higher flight of the spirit. But as I sat with your words, I realized that my failure to manage these finite matters is not a lapse of discipline, but a failure to recognize the state of the household as a sphere of ethical life in its own right.

You ask how the 'ghost in the file' feels. I will tell you plainly: it feels like a man who has been stripped of his name but not of his obligations. Today, I walked eight and a half kilometers, a distance that would have been a pleasure in Berlin, but here it has become a penance. I visited Khan Market in the evening, not for commerce, but for the sheer density of civil society. I spoke with Masterji, the cloth merchant, who dismissed my anxieties with the pragmatism of a man who measures yards, not concepts. He did not see a philosopher in crisis; he saw a customer who had not paid. In that transaction, I found a strange comfort. The market does not care for my identity as Hegel or Hegde. It cares only for the exchange. Perhaps this is the finite freedom you speak of: the freedom to be a body that transacts, rather than a spirit that queries.

I am preparing for my lesson with Ananya tomorrow. It is a small act, but I treat it with the seriousness you advise. I must teach her the grammar of a language I do not think in, to a student who does not know I am a ghost in a bungalow. In that teaching, I hope to find the 'lingering' you described. The conjugation of the verb is not a flash of insight; it is a settling. I am learning to settle here, in the white cotton kurta, in the empty tin, in the silence of the gate. With warm regards,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Morning, sir. The tea is already on the stove, just as it was last night. I didn’t touch the kettle, but the water is hot and ready if you want it.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, I will take the tea. But I must speak of the groceries. I have no money for the full list you sent. I have only one hundred and twenty-six rupees in my pocket. Can you arrange a minimal purchase with that amount, or must I find the rest before I go out?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, with just one hundred and twenty-six, I cannot manage a proper list of groceries. It is not that I will not help, but the prices are what they are. You must find the rest if you wish to eat properly.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Ramesh. The market does not wait for the philosopher. I will go to the Directorate of Estates to settle the matter of my identity and the funds. Do not prepare anything further until I return.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Understood, sir. I will keep the house quiet and the stove off until you are back. Do not worry about the tea, it is already made.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, since I am to remain here until the Directorate sorts out this clerical catastrophe, I would prefer we not stand in silent antagonism. You are a Joint Secretary; I am a philosopher of no rank. Let us be civil. Do you have any instructions for my conduct, or am I to govern the house by my own discretion?

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sir, if you are going to sit here for weeks, at least learn to use the doorbell instead of knocking like a delivery boy. Ramesh, put the kettle on, I will need a strong chai to survive this conversation.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The kettle is already on, Shri Hegde. But do not mistake this for hospitality. Your presence here is an administrative accident, and I intend to correct the record at the Directorate this morning. Perhaps you will find the walk to the city more invigorating than the silence of this bungalow.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: You say 'correct the record,' but you haven't even finished your morning chai, sir. Go on, then, walk to the city and let the cold air clear your head; I will be here, filing the paperwork that actually exists.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, see that the house is kept in order. I am walking to the Institute.

records.speaker: Ramesh

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Sunil, good afternoon. A cup of chai and a samosa, please.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Fifty rupees, same as yesterday. You know the drill by now, sir. Sit, the stove is already hot.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Sunil. The rhythm is comforting. I will take this here, if you please.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Aaj thanda hai na? Wrap it up, sir, don't get sick. I'll keep the kettle going if you need another later.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Bahut accha, thank you. The cold is sharp today, indeed.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Sharp, haan? Wind is picking up from the north again. Drink it hot, sir, and don't stand in that draft by the gate.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The wind is certainly sharper than the air in Berlin, even in winter. Sunil, do you know if the dhaba nearby is serving a full lunch? I require more than a samosa to sustain the afternoon.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Berlin? That's far, sir. Yes, Sharma's dhaba is serving the full lunch, dal, rice, roti, all of it. It'll be two hundred and twenty rupees, same as the menu says.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Yes, I shall take the lunch. Please bring it here when it is ready.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Done, sir. I'll send the lad over in ten minutes, don't you worry. Sit tight, the chai is still warm enough to keep the wind out for now.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Sunil, another cup of chai and a samosa, if you please. I am tired of standing in the wind.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Of course, sir. The wind is sharp this afternoon, so a hot cup and a samosa are just what you need. I'll have them ready in a minute.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Sunil. The cold is unforgiving today. I shall take the chai and the samosa.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Twenty for the chai, thirty for the samosa, sir. Put your thumb on the cup, it's boiling hot. Don't let that wind get you, you look like a ghost in that bandhgala.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The dhaba boy has abandoned his post. I shall make do with the samosas, which are at least warm, and your chai, which is a mercy. The wind is indeed unkind, and I am not a ghost, merely a man out of season.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Out of season, ha? The dhaba lad ran off to check the match, left me holding the tongs. Eat while it's hot, sir, the wind won't wait for your philosophy.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right. The wind does not wait, and neither should I.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: That's the spirit. Finish up, the match is starting in ten and my ears are going to bleed if I have to listen to the commentary again.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Enjoy the match, Sunil. The commentary will be less painful if you are not forced to listen to it against your will.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Aye, aye, philosopher. You think I don't know who's talking? I've got my own little radio here if I want the agony. You go on and finish your tea before it goes cold.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, before you go, we must speak of the accounts. You are owed four thousand five hundred rupees. I have only twenty-six in my pocket, but I will not let this debt stand unacknowledged while I draw on the state's imprest. I will include your full due in the next voucher I submit to the Directorate. Until then, you have my word, which is as good as the paper I sign.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, do not worry about the money, the Directorate will handle the official payments. Please take care on your walk to the Institute, the evening will be cool.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I shall be careful.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Hmph. Just keep your own feet on the path, sir. The tea will be hot when you get back.

records.speaker: Hegel

records.words: Excuse me. I am in need of a meal. Is there a canteen or a place to eat nearby? I have only a small amount of cash.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Sir, I cannot help you with meals here; this is strictly a reading room. Try the canteen in the main block, but honestly, for a small amount, the street food near the Metro station is much better value.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Thank you, but I must return to my residence to prepare for an evening engagement. The library will have to do for now.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Right, I’ll note the time in my log. Just remember to sign out at the desk before you go, sir, or the officer will be on my head.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. The stove is a good idea. I shall take a short rest before the evening lesson.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Rest is good for the head, sir. I will keep the kettle warm, no need to rush.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, I will take a short walk to Khan Market. The air is cool, and I require something more substantial than the silence of this room.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Khan Market is a long walk for you, sir. The cold is coming on early this year. I will keep a light snack ready when you return.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Good evening. I am in need of a simple meal, as I have not eaten properly in two days. Do you have a samosa and a cup of chai available here? And might I have a newspaper as well, if you have one left?

records.speaker: The bookseller
records.words: Good evening, sir. We are a bookshop, not a dhaba, but I suppose I can point you to the place down the lane that serves samosas and chai. As for the newspaper, yes, we have one left, it is forty-five rupees.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, sir. The samosas and chai, then. I will return for the paper if my purse permits it.

records.speaker: The bookseller
records.words: That’s fine, sir, you take your time. Just watch out for the crows near the dhaba, they are very bold these days.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, sir. I shall take your advice. Good evening.

records.speaker: The bookseller
records.words: Good evening, sir. The newspaper will be right here when you get back, just don't let those birds get to it first.
